    Lesson Design Notes

    Last updated on 2026-11-06 | Edit this page

    This page records the design decisions behind the lesson and the reasons for them. It follows the backward design process taught in The Carpentries Collaborative Lesson Development Training: define the learning outcomes, design exercises that check them, write the content, then use what happens in workshops to revise the lesson.

    Audience

    Chosen audience: researchers, analysts and postgraduate students at the University of Edinburgh and partner NHS organisations who write scripts to analyse data but have never used version control. They are novices with Git, though some are competent programmers. See the learner profiles.

    Audience we decided not to design for: learners with no command-line experience at all. The lesson is the final workshop of a two-week programme, so it assumes the shell basics taught earlier. Learners new to the shell should take a shell lesson first.

    Prerequisites and pre-workshop check

    Prerequisites are listed on the home page. To check whether a registrant fits the audience, ask these two questions when they sign up. Self-assessment is unreliable, so ask learners to answer rather than rate themselves.

    1. In a terminal, which command shows the files in the current folder? cd / ls / pwd / I don’t know. Learners who can’t answer ls should take a shell lesson first.
    2. Which of these have you done? I have used Git to make a commit / I have cloned a repository but never committed / I have never used Git. This shows the mix of experience in the group, so the instructor can plan extension tasks for learners who already use Git.

    Lesson objectives and how episodes map to them

    By the end of the lesson, learners will be able to:

    1. Track changes to their own project with Git, and inspect and restore earlier versions of their work.
    2. Share a project on GitLab and collaborate with others in a shared repository, resolving rejected pushes and merge conflicts.
    3. Use branches to keep experimental work separate, and tags to mark the version of their code used for a result.
    Episode Lesson objective Objectives Challenges
    1. Why Version Control? 1 3 1
    2. Configuring Git 1 4 3
    3. Recording Changes Locally 1 6 4
    4. Working with Remote Repositories 2 4 4
    5. Using Git with a GUI (RStudio) 1, 2 5 0
    6. Collaborating 2 4 3
    7. Exploring History 1 5 4
    8. Ignoring Things 1 3 1
    9. Branching and Tagging 3 7 5

    Narrative and example data

    Learners build a single project, MyProject, through episodes 3 to 6. It contains a small genomics dataset (Data/data.csv, a tidy table of variant calls from the Data Carpentry genomics workshop data) and a short Python script (Src/hello.py) that reads it. The story is a researcher putting an existing analysis under version control, then sharing it with a collaborator.

    This scenario was chosen because it matches what the learners do: they already have scripts and data, and the problem is keeping track of versions and sharing them safely. The dataset is real but small, so it doesn’t distract from Git itself.

    Exercises

    Exercises are written to check episode objectives, and every exercise has a worked solution. They use a mix of formats suited to novices: predict-the-output questions, multiple-choice questions, and short hands-on tasks in the learners’ own project. In a hybrid workshop the online helper monitors exercise progress for learners joining remotely.

    Life cycle

    Stage What changed
    Pre-alpha Lesson created from the Carpentries Workbench template (June 2025)
    Beta Lesson taught as part of the Introduction to Data Science programme. Learner profiles, prerequisites, lesson objectives, instructor notes and design notes added; collaboration exercises added to episode 6

    Changes made after teaching

    • Learners asked for more time at the end to practise on a realistic example, and a peer observer suggested extension tasks for learners who finish quickly. Tiered exercises and a closing worked example are planned.
    • The peer observer noticed that the instructor sometimes spoke to the class before an exercise timer ended. Instructors should stay quiet while learners work on an exercise.

    Known gaps

    These are the next steps for the lesson, judged against the Collaborative Lesson Development Training guidance:

    • Exercises for every objective. Episode 5 has no challenges, and episodes 1 and 8 have one challenge for three objectives.
    • Number of objectives per episode. The guidance suggests 2–4. Episodes 3, 5, 7 and 9 have more, so their objectives could be grouped, or episode 9 split into separate Branching and Tagging episodes.
    • Skill-based objectives. Some objectives name a command rather than a task, for example “Initialise a repository with git init”.
    • One narrative throughout. Episodes 8 and 9 use their own example files (secret.txt, summary.py) rather than continuing MyProject.
    • Missing images in episodes 4, 5, 7 and 8.
